simulation_brief.primary_tension: institutional efficiency versus community identity and access
simulation_brief.summary: A fictional school board is considering whether to merge two under-enrolled high schools. No final decision has been made at T0. Key pressures include enrollment decline, budget concerns, school identity, travel logistics, staffing implications, and community legitimacy. The initialization should remain balanced, with plausible branches including merger, delay, compromise, and backlash.
uncertainty_notes: No named schools, district size, or exact enrollment figures are provided.
Specific board member positions are not stated at T0.
No explicit fiscal emergency or legal deadline is given, so pressure exists without requiring immediate crisis.

sociology_baseline.note: Stakeholders are somewhat open to persuasion when proposals are concrete, but identity-linked views are sticky.
Visible triggers such as a draft vote date, mascot loss, or route changes could rapidly increase turnout and protest.
Undecided families and pragmatic teachers may hold back until details are clearer.
School-specific social ties and feeder communities reinforce in-group narratives.
Participation is more likely after repeated cues from parents, teachers, boosters, and peers.
Existing school identity is a major organizing force in attitudes toward merger.
Sustained attention may soften without a hearing, leak, recommendation, or vote schedule.

sociology_prompt_influences.description: School names, teams, traditions, and community attachment are likely to frame reactions beyond pure cost analysis.
Stakeholders care whether the board appears transparent, consultative, and even-handed.

Low enrollment creates an efficiency rationale that keeps merger options live even without consensus.
